tm-001-thermal: Spacecraft thermal control keeps every component inside the temperature band it was qualified for. In vacuum there is no convection, so essentially all waste heat must eventually leave the vehicle as infrared radiation. Passive techniques are preferred wherever they suffice, because they consume no power and have nothing to fail. Multilayer insulation blankets, typically a stack of aluminised polyimide sheets separated by a low-conductance net, reduce parasitic heat leak between the interior and the external environment. Surface finishes are selected for their ratio of solar absorptivity to infrared emissivity; a low ratio keeps a sunlit surface cool, while a high ratio helps a component reject heat to deep space. Active techniques are introduced only when the passive design cannot hold the band across all mission phases. These include electrical resistance heaters under thermostatic or software control, single-phase pumped fluid loops that move heat from dense avionics to an external panel, and deployable radiators that increase the available rejection area once the vehicle has reached its operating attitude. Radiator area is almost always sized by the worst-case hot condition rather than the average, because a design that survives the hottest attitude will generally tolerate the cold case with heater power that is comparatively cheap to supply.
tm-002-power: An Earth-orbiting spacecraft normally generates electrical power with photovoltaic arrays and stores it in secondary batteries to carry the vehicle through eclipse. Array output degrades over the mission from radiation damage, thermal cycling, and contamination, so the beginning-of-life capacity is specified with margin against the end-of-life requirement rather than the nominal demand. Battery sizing depends principally on the depth of discharge the chemistry tolerates at the required cycle count; a low Earth orbit vehicle passing through roughly fifteen eclipses per day accumulates cycles far more quickly than a geostationary vehicle, which experiences eclipse seasons only twice a year. Power distribution is regulated on a main bus, and loads are grouped so that a fault in one branch can be isolated without dropping the whole vehicle. Peak power tracking extracts the maximum available from the array as its operating point drifts with temperature and degradation.
tm-003-attitude: Attitude determination and control establishes where a vehicle is pointing and drives it to where it needs to point. Determination typically fuses several sensor types, because each is strong where another is weak. Star trackers give the most accurate absolute attitude but need an unobstructed view and can be blinded by the Sun or a bright limb. Sun sensors are coarse but robust and are often the basis of a safe mode. Rate gyroscopes provide high-bandwidth angular rate but drift over time and must be periodically corrected against an absolute reference. Actuation is usually provided by reaction wheels for fine pointing, with magnetic torque rods or thrusters used to desaturate the wheels once stored momentum approaches their limit. Control authority must be sized against the dominant disturbance torques, which at low altitude are aerodynamic and gravity gradient, and at high altitude are solar radiation pressure and magnetic residual dipole.
tm-004-comms: A spacecraft communications link is designed by accounting for every gain and loss between the transmitter and the receiver output. The link budget starts from transmitter power, adds antenna gains, subtracts free-space path loss, pointing loss, atmospheric absorption and implementation losses, and compares the result against the signal-to-noise ratio the chosen modulation and coding require. Free-space path loss grows with the square of both distance and frequency, which is why deep-space missions use large ground apertures and highly directional spacecraft antennas. Error-correcting codes buy back several decibels of required signal-to-noise at the cost of bandwidth and latency. A margin of at least three decibels over the required ratio is conventional, to absorb weather, ageing and the difference between predicted and measured performance.
